title: Challenge: Slow/Fast Pointers

writing.exampleCaption: Complete std-only slow-fast program for its typed teaching fixture. Parsing and output construction are separate from the core algorithm.
writing.explanation:
Each pair of consumed elements advances the middle one position. The worked program demonstrates this invariant on an independent fixture, so you can study the implementation before predicting the challenge result.

For teaching input `[1,2,3,4,5]`, the worked program returns `3`. Its functions are complete and use only std. Adapt the same state transitions to the visible challenge input `[4,8,15,16,23,42]`; predict that result before opening the answer reveal. The precise contract is: Return the middle value; for even length choose the second middle.

Return canonical output: lowercase booleans, decimal integers without leading zeros, comma-separated values and semicolon-separated groups, with no extra whitespace or final newline. Whole medians use integer form and half medians use .5. Textual sentinels such as none and # retain their stated meaning. String and character-grid fixtures use ASCII unless the lesson explicitly specifies Unicode scalar values.

Solve the exact task, not just the visible example: Return the middle value; for even length choose the second middle. On input `[4,8,15,16,23,42]`, predict the output before opening the answer reveal. The revealed output is a test oracle for this case, while private checks exercise other legal cases. Start by stating the input grammar and output format in your own words. Parse the complete input, including surrounding whitespace, before relying on any convenient positions in the example.

Build the solution around one maintained claim: Advance pointers at different rates so relative motion reveals a midpoint or cycle. Decide what state represents that claim, how it is initialized, what a single update does, and when the algorithm stops. Two positions move according to a monotone fact: after one comparison, some candidates can be ruled out permanently. Name that fact. Trace the visible input by hand and record at least two intermediate states, not only the final answer. If the trace cannot justify your predicted output, there is a gap between the idea and the implementation.

Check both correctness and cost. The intended bound is O(n) time · O(1) space; explain which operation dominates it and how many times the input can trigger that operation. Test pointers meeting, crossing, duplicate values, and the smallest valid input; many off-by-one errors hide there. Add one small case that should succeed, one boundary case, and one case chosen to challenge the invariant. Compare your hand result with the program's result, then use a failing case to fix the earliest incorrect state transition rather than patching the final output.
writing.feedback: For this input the result is `5`. Each pair of consumed elements advances the middle one position. Compare this independent fixture with the worked trace: For six values [4,8,15,16,23,42], the slow positions after three paired advances are 1,2,3. Index 3 contains 16, the second of the two middle elements. A one-element input performs no advance.
